result: All four SNARE complexes (neuronal, GLUT4, endosomal, and yeast) assemble via the same conserved step-wise zippering mechanism with three sequential steps: slow NTD association, fast CTD zippering, and rapid LD zippering, proceeding through common intermediate states (t-SNARE state, half-zippered state, and LD-unfolded state).
evaluation: Claims C2, C49, C70, C81, and C82 are directly supported by single-molecule optical tweezers experiments (C56-C69) showing similar force-extension curves, binary transitions, and extension changes across all four SNARE complexes. The structural intermediates were confirmed by model fitting (C71-C72) and truncation experiments (C73-C74). The data consistently demonstrate a conserved assembly pathway.

result: The CTD zippering energy varies significantly among SNARE complexes (neuronal: 27 kBT, GLUT4: 23 kBT, endosomal: 16 kBT, yeast: 13 kBT) and is concentrated at the C-terminal portion of the CTD, creating a polarized energy distribution with higher energy density at the C-terminus.
evaluation: Claims C3, C50, and C83 are supported by quantitative measurements from constant-force experiments (C5, Figure 5) and energy landscape analysis. The polarized distribution (C4, C154) is derived from the position of transition states (C87) and force calculations (C121). The measurements are internally consistent and validated against prior work (C84).

result: SNARE complexes share a conserved zippering pathway and polarized energy release for efficient membrane fusion, but generate different amounts of zippering energy to regulate fusion kinetics in different cellular contexts.
evaluation: This integrative conclusion (C5, C6, C166, C167) is supported by the demonstrated conservation of mechanism (C2, C49) combined with the measured differences in CTD energy (C3, C83). The functional interpretation regarding fusion kinetics regulation (C153) is supported by the energy measurements and discussion of different fusion processes (C9, C10, C146), though direct kinetic measurements of fusion were not performed in this study.

result: The chimeric SNARE construct, where cognate SNARE proteins are joined into one polypeptide with spacer sequences, forms proper helical bundles and is functionally equivalent to wild-type SNAREs in membrane fusion assays and single-molecule measurements.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by multiple validation experiments: circular dichroism showing alpha-helical structure (C52), gel filtration confirming proper assembly (C52), lipid mixing assays demonstrating fusion activity (C53), and consistency with prior measurements using different constructs (C55, C84). The spacer sequences have minimal effects on folding energy and kinetics (C54, C85).

result: Force-extension curves reveal that SNARE complexes undergo sequential unfolding via two reversible binary transitions (CTD and LD) and irreversible NTD unfolding, with transitions remaining cooperative at all forces tested but shifting to unfolded states at higher forces.
evaluation: Claims C56-C59, C67-C68 describe the fundamental experimental observations from optical tweezers measurements. The binary nature of transitions is demonstrated by two-peak extension histograms (C67, Figure 5B, 6B), and the sequential unfolding is shown in force-extension curves (Figure 2A). The interpretation of continuous vs. discontinuous extension changes (C57-C58) is standard for single-molecule force spectroscopy.

result: The half-zippered state structure was determined for all four SNARE complexes, with R SNAREs unzipped to positions within 3 amino acids of the ionic layer (neuronal: -1, GLUT4: +3, endosomal: +1, yeast: +3), and an additional transient t-SNARE intermediate was observed during unfolding.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by quantitative model fitting of force-extension curves (described in Methods and C57). The structural assignments are validated by the similar extension changes across complexes (C69) and confirmed by truncation experiments (C73-C74). The t-SNARE intermediate (C80) is identified from extension positions and observed in varying frequencies (C78-C79).

result: The CTD folding energy barrier is minimal or absent at zero force for all SNARE complexes, with transition states located between the third and sixth hydrophobic layers, indicating that fusion rate is not limited by intrinsic CTD folding and that half-zippered state stability is strongly force-dependent.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are derived from extrapolation of force-dependent measurements (Figure 5C-D) using energy landscape modeling. The transition state positions (C87) are determined from force-dependent rate analysis. The inference about fusion rate limitation (C88) is reasonable given the small barriers, though it remains an interpretation rather than direct measurement.

result: The linker domain (LD) transitions are reversible, binary, and fast across all four SNARE complexes, occurring in narrow force ranges (6-8.6 pN) lower than CTD transitions (10.1-18.5 pN), with LD zippering outputting less energy than CTD zippering, making CTD the major power stroke for membrane fusion.
evaluation: Claims C91-C92, C98-C99 are supported by constant-force measurements (Figure 6) showing similar LD transition characteristics across complexes. The force ranges and energy comparisons (Table 1) directly support C92 and C98. The conclusion that CTD is the major power stroke (C99) follows logically from the energy comparison and is supported by citation to prior work.

result: NTD association initiates at 12.5 nm membrane separation with small opposing force (2-5 pN), proceeds through coil-to-helix propagation of t-SNARE, and forms the half-zippered state at 9.7 nm, releasing ~26 kBT that can be used for vesicle docking and priming.
evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are derived from energy landscape calculations combining measured SNARE energies with membrane interaction energies from prior SFA measurements (C100-C103). The calculations are methodologically sound and based on established biophysical principles. However, the specific distances and energies depend on the membrane interaction model parameters (Equation 1), which introduces some uncertainty.

result: CTD zippering from the half-zippered state is directly coupled to membrane fusion, drawing membranes from 9.7 nm to 1 nm against large forces, reducing the fusion energy barrier to 7.4 kBT per SNARE complex, consistent with a fusion rate of ~600 s⁻¹.
evaluation: Claims C110-C114 are supported by energy landscape calculations (Figure 7B-D) that integrate measured CTD energies (C83) with membrane interaction energies. The calculated barrier (C113) and predicted fusion rate (C114) are internally consistent with the model assumptions. However, the fusion rate prediction assumes a maximum rate of 10⁶ s⁻¹ and was not directly validated experimentally.

result: SNARE zippering produces increasing force output as CTD zippers toward the C-terminus, with the first two-thirds generating 8 pN average force and the last one-third generating 32 pN, creating an energy barrier at ~5 nm that results in the binary CTD transition and polarized energy distribution.
evaluation: Claims C119-C121, C124 are supported by calculations from the energy landscape model (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The force calculations are mathematically correct given the measured energy distribution. The connection between force application and energy barrier formation (C123-C124) is supported by thermodynamic principles and prior literature citations.

result: Alternative energy landscapes with N-terminal polarized energy distribution would greatly stabilize the half-zippered state but increase the fusion barrier to 24 kBT (vs. 7.4 kBT for wild-type), demonstrating that C-terminal polarized energy distribution is essential for efficient membrane fusion and that continuous assembly leads to poor coupling.
evaluation: Claims C125-C131 are supported by comparative calculations using alternative energy distributions (Figure 7B, dashed lines). The calculations show that C-terminal polarization consistently produces lower fusion barriers across different membrane parameters (C128). This computational analysis effectively demonstrates the functional importance of the observed energy distribution, though experimental validation of the alternative scenario is not possible.

result: The identification of half-zippered intermediates in all four SNARE complexes demonstrates that SNAREs follow a common zippering mechanism rather than all-or-none or continuous layer-by-layer assembly, with the half-zippered complex being intrinsic to SNAREs and functionally important for membrane fusion.
evaluation: Claims C132-C134, C136, C138 are well-supported by the experimental identification of half-zippered states across all complexes (C71-C72) and prior literature (C135). The rejection of alternative mechanisms (C133) is justified by the observed binary transitions and intermediates. The functional importance (C138) is supported by citations to prior work and unpublished mutational studies (C137).

result: The large difference in CTD zippering energy between SNARE complexes (12-14 kBT difference) suggests that different numbers of SNARE complexes are required for different fusion processes in vivo, contributing to the variation in fusion rates, though in vitro reconstituted fusion shows similar rates due to uncontrolled SNARE numbers.
evaluation: Claims C149-C153 present a reasonable interpretation of how energy differences relate to SNARE stoichiometry and fusion kinetics. The logic is supported by the measured energy differences (C83) and prior literature on SNARE numbers in vivo (C150) vs. in vitro (C151-C152). However, this remains an inference rather than direct experimental demonstration, as SNARE numbers were not measured in this study.

result: SNAREs contain a built-in automatic transmission system that adjusts force output to accommodate the large force changes required for membrane fusion, ensuring efficient and tight coupling between SNARE zippering and membrane fusion by producing highest forces at the C-termini.
evaluation: Claims C156-C157, C168 represent the central mechanistic conclusion integrating the polarized energy distribution (C154), force calculations (C119-C121), and membrane interaction requirements (C40-C42). This conclusion is well-supported by the experimental data and energy landscape analysis, though the "automatic transmission" is a conceptual model rather than a directly measured property.

result: For GLUT4-storage vesicle fusion, which takes ~1 minute after insulin triggering, the observed fusion rate is probably limited by slow NTD association rather than fast CTD zippering, suggesting insulin mainly regulates steps upstream of NTD association.
evaluation: Claims C147-C148 are speculative inferences based on the measured kinetics (slow NTD, fast CTD) and prior literature on GSV fusion timing (C146). While the reasoning is plausible, no direct experiments were performed to test this hypothesis. The claims represent reasonable speculation but lack experimental validation in the context of insulin signaling or GSV fusion.

result: The half-zippered structure may be more ancient in SNARE evolution than regulatory proteins targeting it, may have more conserved function than previously thought, and may be the target of SM-family proteins essential for SNARE-mediated fusion.
evaluation: Claims C139-C140 are evolutionary inferences based on the observed conservation across species (yeast to mammals), but no phylogenetic or evolutionary analysis was performed. Claim C143 about SM proteins is speculative (marked as "SPECULATION" in evidence_type) and supported only by citations to prior work, not by experiments in this study. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work.

result: The external force applied by optical tweezers mimics the opposing force from membranes, though with different force constants (0.1 pN/nm for optical trap vs. 7.1 pN/nm for membrane force), making membrane repulsive force an integral component of SNARE assembly and regulation.
evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this principle. Claims C115-C116, C118 are supported by the energy landscape calculations showing how membrane forces stabilize the half-zippered state differently than optical trap forces. The comparison of force constants (C116) is quantitatively derived from the models. This validates the experimental approach while acknowledging its limitations.

result: A highly conserved phenylalanine residue in the C-terminal region of v-SNAREs across all four complexes is critical for tight association and the binary CTD transition, with its substitution to alanine abolishing both the CTD transition in vitro and exocytosis.
evaluation: Claim C162 is supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). Claims C163-C164 are supported by unpublished work (manuscript in preparation) and prior literature (C164). While the unpublished data cannot be fully evaluated, the prior published work on exocytosis (C164) and the sequence conservation (C162) provide strong supporting evidence for the functional importance of this residue.

result: Truncation experiments on yeast SNARE complex show that LD truncation eliminates the LD transition but not CTD transition, while CTD truncation abolishes both transitions, confirming the derived intermediate structures.
evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are directly supported by experimental data from truncation mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). These experiments provide critical validation of the structural assignments for the intermediate states and demonstrate that the domains fold independently in the expected sequence. This is strong supporting evidence for the structural model.

result: The NTD is mechanically more stable than CTD, unfolding after 10-10⁵ CTD transitions, with unfolding being irreversible (remaining unfolded >50 s), indicating a large energy barrier for NTD association, and both CTD and LD fold rapidly (>50 s⁻¹) even at equilibrium forces.
evaluation: Claims C63, C76-C77 are supported by direct observations from force-extension curves (Figure 2B) showing the relative stability and irreversibility of NTD unfolding. Claim C75 is supported by rate measurements (Figures 5-6) and comparison to prior literature on coiled-coil proteins. These observations are consistent across all four SNARE complexes and represent robust experimental findings.

result: The association of the N-terminal half of VAMP2 to the N-terminal t-SNARE triggers folding of the t-SNARE C-terminal domain, which then serves as a template for fast and energetic VAMP2 zippering.
evaluation: Claims C160-C161 are supported by citations to recent prior work (Li et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2012). While not directly demonstrated in this study, these findings from prior literature are used to inform the structural model for NTD association (C105) and are consistent with the observed fast CTD zippering kinetics. The citations provide adequate support for these mechanistic details.
